Christopher | 10:14 AM on August 01, 2026 Photo credit Justin Merriman The United States of America was founded as a Judeo-Christian nation. This is an indisputable historical fact. Those who claim the First Amendment was never intended to allow prayer in school should know that the authors of that glorious amendment returned home from the Constitutional Convention of 1789 to pass laws declaring official religions for their entire states. So, I think they would have been fine with our young adults gathering at the flagpole, before school starts, for an unofficial prayer. Advertisement For nearly 200 years, little changed about our self-perception as a religious nation. The cultural regression of the 1960s dented that, but America is still the most religious of all western nations. And in an age of open genocide against Christians in the third world, the unchecked onslaught of Islam against everything civilized, and the entropic decay of post-Christian Europe into nihilistic resignation, our distinction is more important than ever. The Founding Fathers were largely Protestant. But the allure of our nation, both before and after, attracted Lutherans, Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, Methodists, Baptists, Calvinists, and Presbyterians. Other denominations, such as Pentecostals and Mormons, are American-born sects. And while all these denominations differ in varying degrees in their eschatological approaches to the faith, one thing is certain. Every one of these denominations was born from a deep and sincere effort to get closer to God. None of these denominations evolved from a group of slackers looking for a “shortcut” to God. None of them arose from an attempt to treat Christianity as a smorgasbord, where its congregants pick and choose which aspects of the religion they like and leave the rest. This Old Country Buffet approach is a purely modern perversion, with the added annoyance that its practitioners make sure to tell everyone in their vicinity that, “I’m not religious, I’m spiritual. ” But more on that tomorrow. Advertisement The point is, multiple overlapping (and sometimes competing) denominations living side by side in relative peace wasn’t always the norm. In Europe, it led to the French civil wars and the pan-continental Thirty Years’ War. But here in America, there has been very little, if any, inter-Christian violence. Racists and leftists, not Christians, attacked churches, both during the Jim Crow era and today. But that doesn’t make us faultless. Read through the Comments section of any article about Christianity and you’ll find Christians of differing denominations at each other’s throats. Sometimes it’s expressed in crass mockery. Other times it's masked underneath benign theological jargon. But the message is the same. Your church is corrupt and heretical, whereas mine gets it 100% right and is flawless. No, YOUR church is corrupt and heretical, whereas MINE gets it 100% right and is flawless. Can we please stop our pathetic little slap fight? No church, including my own, gets it 100% right and is flawless. It requires a grotesque lack of humility for any of us to assume we can wrap our pea brains around the infinite mysteries of God and His designs with any more precision than the next congregation of sad, ignorant creatures in the next church down the street. And it’s not like our “leaders” are providing sound guidance. The leaders of the Catholic Church support the unfettered mass importation of illegal criminals into hitherto peaceful societies. The leaders of the Anglican Church pre-emptively surrendered to Islam. The leaders of the Russian Orthodox Church (the biggest Orthodox denomination) are Putin sycophants. Advertisement The leaders of the Presbyterian Church long ago decided that the logical way forward was to turn itself into a blue-haired, nonbinary pride parade. And the leaders of the United Methodist Church are eager to follow suit. In short, too many churches have turned away from love the sinner but hate the sin. They now preach normalize the sin and deify the sinner. Related: The Insidious Motivation Underlying Trans Ideology (Hint: It Isn't Concern for Civil Rights) But if our churches have collectively strayed from the path to God, it is due to the politicization of religion and the desire of church leaders to conform to the latest Quinnipiac poll rather than to the message of the Gospel. It is not due to our centuries-old eschatological divergences, and we need to stop behaving as if those divergences are cause for conflict. My utter disappointment with the current pope and his immediate predecessor aside, I’m a practicing Catholic because, through inference and deduction via my extremely limited understanding of the world around me, I found Catholicism to be the best path to God. But does that make me a “better” Christian than non-Catholics? Martin Luther King Jr. not only successfully led the movement for civil rights, but he did so with a message of peace and racial brotherhood in an era when so many other black leaders were screaming for the exact opposite. Oh, but he was a Baptist. Does that make him wrong and me right? Advertisement Andrew van der Bijl, also known as “God’s Smuggler,” spent decades smuggling Bibles to Christians behind the Iron Curtain, and he later founded the Open Doors foundation. Oh, but he was a Methodist. Does that make him wrong and me right? Elizaveta Skobtsova was a Latvian refugee living in Paris during the Nazi occupation, during which time she used her home to shelter Jews and sneak them out of the country. After the Gestapo arrested her, she was sent to the Ravensbruck concentration camp. She ended up in the gas chamber after she volunteered to take the place of a Jewish prisoner. Oh, but she was Orthodox. Does that make her wrong and me right? Thomas Byles was an Oxford graduate living in Essex, England. In April 1912, he sailed for America to attend his brother’s wedding. While crossing the Atlantic, disaster struck and his ship sank. Survivors last saw Byles praying with roughly a hundred passengers who were stuck on board. Byles himself didn’t need to be there. He was twice offered a place on the lifeboats, and twice he refused. He chose to give his seat to someone else, and went down with the RMS Titanic . Oh, but he was Catholic priest. Does that make him wrong and you right? Anyone with young kids knows that they color pictures for you. Your young son hands you a scribbled mess that he says is a lion in the jungle. Your young daughter hands you a scribbled mess that she says is daddy brushing his teeth. And those two scribbled messes mean more to you than anything, because they represent an act of pure love that your kids created for you. Advertisement To them, you are God. But sometimes the kids fight about whose picture is better, about which picture you will like more, etc., and the act of love devolves into a yelling match fueled by pride. At which point you intervene and stop their pathetic little slap fight. And you remind your kids that both acts of love are acknowledged and cherished. Yes, you realize that one might grasp artistic ideas and talents more than the other, but that’s not the point. You’re their creator, and you want not only for both of them to know how much you love them, but you also want them to love each other as brother and sister. And so it is with us. No gift or prayer or homage to God will ever compare to the act of creation with which He blessed us. Catholic and Protestant, Orthodox and Methodist, Baptist and Presbyterian, we are all using the nanosecond of time we have to claw our way through the darkness and try to derive but a sliver of wisdom from an infinite abyss. The most we can offer up is our own scribbled messes based on our extremely limited comprehension of who God is and what He wants. So let’s stop our pathetic little slap fight. When the congregation down the road offers up a scribbled mess that doesn’t look exactly like our scribbled mess, we need to overcome our pride and concede that God will recognize their loving devotion just as much as He recognizes ours. https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-ste.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JExS This is Wadephul's fourth visit to Ukraine since taking office 16 months ago Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS Advertisement Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul condemned Russia 's escalating drone and missile assault on Ukraine on Saturday, as he arrived in Kyiv to demonstrate Berlin's continued support. "Ukraine is celebrating its 35th Independence Day these days. At the same time, Putin's rockets and drones are attacking the country more relentlessly than ever before," he said on X. "The Russian attacks are deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure such as power and heating supply," he wrote, adding Germany was "working to support Ukraine in its winter preparations." Ukraine will mark the 35th anniversary of its independence from the Soviet Union on August 24. This will be its fifth straight independence day under Russia's invasion , which began in February 2022. Wadephul's visit to Ukraine comes amid increasing Russian air assaults and what he called "indiscriminate murder of civilians." On Saturday morning, drone and missile attacks killed at least two people in Kyiv and the southern city of Zaporizhzhia. Earlier this week, at least 16 people were killed in Russian missile strikes on Kyiv. On Friday, an attack on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih killed at least 15 people and injured more than 100. Kryvyi Rih is Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown Image: REUTERS Ukraine continues attacks on Russian infrastructure facilities Ukraine has been increasingly targeting Russian oil and gas production and processing sites in recent months. Overnight, Ukrainian drones hit an industrial facility as well as a warehouse owned by popular online retailer Ozon in Russia's southwest Samara region. In ⁠a post on Telegram, Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said that several people had been wounded in the strikes. He did not name the ​industrial facility struck, but Ukraine's military said it had struck the region's Novokuibyshevsk refinery, ​causing a fire. Ukrainian drones also struck other regions in Russia, with regional officials having said that at least six civilians were killed in strikes. While Kyiv has stepped up its strikes on Russia, it is running short of air defense units , leading to more casualties at home. Russia launches missile and drone barrage on Kyiv To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What else did Wadephul say during his visit to Kyiv? The German foreign minister, after reaching Kyiv via a special train, told reporters that July and August had been the deadliest months for Ukrainian civilians in more than four years. "Never before has Russia fired more missiles at its neighboring country," Wadephul said. "We see the suffering, we see how this country has struggled, and we will continue to support this country." "We stand on Ukraine's side," he added. "It will win this military confrontation." Wadephul went on to pledge further support for Ukraine, which is set to face another winter with more attacks expected on its energy infrastructure. "No country invests as much in military and financial support for Ukraine as Germany," Wadephul said, on his fourth visit to the war-torn nation in 16 months. Speaking alongside his Ukrainian counterpart Andriy Sybiga, he said Russia's "brutal war of aggression... has in no way abated." "On the contrary, Putin has even increased the intensity of his war. He is deliberately terrorising civilians, attacking civilian infrastructure with rockets and swarms of drones," Wadephul said. Despite the recent escalation, Wadephul also expressed hope that Russia could be brought to the negotiating table, even as diplomatic efforts have stalled . But it will not be enough.’ Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘Ratcliffe’s trip was necessary, especially in light of Russia’s reckless grey-zone operations in Europe. But it will not be enough.’ Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images Opinion Ukraine The wars in Ukraine and Iran are becoming dangerously enmeshed Christopher S Chivvis As the Trump administration refuses to end its war in Iran, it is steering into the storm, not out of it Thu 3 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 06.03 EDT Share R ussia hasn’t yet killed large numbers of Europeans outside Ukraine, but it’s getting closer. The night of 4-5 August, an airport bus driver discovered an armed drone lying near the tarmac of the Leipzig-Halle airport, which is a central hub of Europe’s logistical support to Ukraine’s war effort. A cargo jet, meanwhile, may have struck a second drone shortly after takeoff, forcing an abrupt landing, and investigators found a third drone laden with military explosives nearby. In 2024, incendiary devices hidden in parcels ignited in DHL cargo at the same airport. Had these detonated in the air, a major air catastrophe and large-scale civilian casualties would have ensued, probably resulting in a broader war. The most recent incident may be what prompted the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to get on a plane for Moscow last week. There, according to reports, he warned his counterparts against attacks on Nato territory, urged them to curb support for Iran, argued that escalation in Ukraine would backfire, and pressed for a deal with Ukraine to end the war. Patriot missiles have been a godsend for Ukraine against Putin, but they’re running out. Kyiv needs help and fast | Jack Watling Read more Ratcliffe’s trip is unlikely to have much impact on the Kremlin’s plans for an escalation against Ukraine in the coming months – but it is further evidence of the dangerous and growing enmeshment of the Iran and Ukraine wars. Sending Ratcliffe to Moscow is a logical choice for the White House, given the substantial role the intelligence services play in Putin’s government and justifiable concern that he may be getting too-rosy assessments of the war from his own team. The attempt at diplomacy is to be applauded. Nevertheless, the Trump administration’s refusal to end the war with Iran is working at cross purposes with their effort to end the war in Ukraine. They are steering into the storm, not out of it. One of the reasons for Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow, according to the Washington Post, was to dispel the Kremlin’s belief that the Trump White House was distracted from Ukraine by Iran. Good luck with that. The reporting on the severe depletion of US interceptor stocks from the war on Iran is so extensive it can only have encouraged Vladimir Putin to launch even more deadly missile strikes against Ukraine’s defenseless population. Ukraine, for its part, has sent 228 specialists and truckloads of drones to assist the Gulf states in their defense against Iranian missile strikes, prompting at least one Iranian lawmaker to declare Ukraine fair game for its own attacks. And Ukraine struck an Iranian commercial vessel in late July. Russia has meanwhile provided Iran with battlefield intelligence that make its strikes more deadly. Moscow has, of course, also long benefited from Iranian-designed drones to attack Ukraine. Both conflicts are getting worse and going nowhere at the same time. True, Putin is in a pinch, with an economy badly damaged by Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, but the pinch will just as easily prompt Russia’s leader toward escalation as it will restraint – especially if he sees the US distracted again in the Middle East and believes he has a window of opportunity to deal a crushing death blow to Kyiv. Putin, like Zelensky, like Trump, and like the Iranian leadership, faces the same sunk-cost dilemma that has led so many of history’s wartime leaders to double down on fruitless military operations – from Alcibiades in Sicily, to Napoleon in Russia , to LBJ in Vietnam. If today’s leaders follow suit, the costs and escalation risks will mount while the conflicts fuse further. Meanwhile, Xi Jinping and Putin met on Monday and will join Iran’s leaders in Bishkek this week for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. They will discuss their plan to link their energy markets even more closely and probably condemn the new “economic offensive” that the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced last week to intensify pressure on Iran. Beijing may not want to see either war continue, but it also does not want to see Russia or Iran lose outright, and it is still in a strong position to avoid this outcome by helping the Iranians and Russians stave off the worst effects of the war on their economies and populations. Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding Read more Ratcliffe’s trip was necessary, especially in light of Russia’s reckless grey-zone operations in Europe . But it will not be enough. His predecessor, Bill Burns, once went to Moscow in an effort to warn Russia against attacking Ukraine. That intervention fell on deaf ears, as Ratcliffe’s also will. Clearer plans to end both wars through more positive inducements are badly needed. To start, Washington should settle with Iran by unfreezing assets and offering sanctions relief in exchange for a real ceasefire and a framework arrangement for joint control of the strait by the littoral powers. It can then work to mitigate the consequences of this loss with a major push to diversify energy supplies – through alternative routes out of the region, alternative sources such as Venezuela, and a push on renewables. Ukraine, meanwhile, needs to become more serious about neutrality. It also needs a real debate about whether hanging on to the remainder of the Donbass it controls is worth indefinitely perpetuating the war. In the conclusion to his recent book, The Coming Storm, which traces the parallels between today’s world and the world on the eve of the first world war, the historian Odd Arne Westad writes: “A key lesson of the world before 1914 is that regional conflicts, long left unresolved, can be the powder kegs that set off a global conflagration.” As the Iran and Ukraine conflicts intertwine without an end in sight, the world’s leaders should take such warnings far more seriously. But without real pressure from their citizens, they may not. History is not doomed to repeat itself. But you don’t need to be a renowned historian to recognize the dangers the world is throwing up before us, nor to lament the failure of our leaders to calm these storms. Christopher S Chivvis is a senior fellow and director of the American Statecraft Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Announces Time Charter Contract for m/v Astarte With Aquavita MV Baltazar officially named in Fremantle, Western Australia Weekly Dry Time Charter Estimates, September 16 2026 Japan’s Minister of the Environment and Other Government Officials Visit ICO Terminal at the Port of Zeebrugge, Belgium Kalmar and ICTSI continue collaboration with hybrid straddle carrier order for new South Luzon Container Terminal Danube congestion continues to tighten general cargo and small dry bulk vessel availability in the Black Sea in International Shipping News 03/09/2026 P ersistent congestion in the Danube River has been lowering vessel availability in the Black Sea, particularly for smaller general cargo tonnage, while also affecting some dry bulk vessels. Prolonged delays are likely to keep regional freight rates high throughout the grain export season. Ukraine’s exports have come under pressure as repeated Russian attacks have disrupted operations at its main Black Sea ports in the Odesa region. The country’s deep-sea ports historically handle most of its grain exports; however, the latest Russian strikes targeted export infrastructure in the region, forcing cargo to be rerouted through lower-capacity Danube ports, including the Port Reni and Izmail. As a result, it is creating massive congestion near the Sulina port, with the current fleet mainly comprising smaller general cargo vessels. Few dry bulk vessels are also caught up in the congestion, putting pressure on vessel availability in the region. As Ukrainian grain exports now rely on the Danube corridor, infrastructure and navigational constraints limit vessel throughput and reduce effective fleet availability, supporting freight markets in the Black Sea. Regional fleet availability under pressure Vessel queues at Sulina remain high, with around 70 vessels, including dry bulk and general cargo, awaiting transit, with limited daily passage capacity to Ukrainian Danube ports. Around 52 (above 2.6 kdwt) general cargo vessels, totalling about 280 kdwt, are currently waiting outside Ukrainian Danube ports. Out of the global fleet of around 30.6 mdwt in this size segment, about 7 mdwt, or 23%, is typically deployed in the Black Sea region, including Russian ports. Although these waiting-zone vessels represent only 4% of the Black Sea fleet (up to 10k dwt), tightening the effective vessel supply, as ongoing delays remove a major portion of the fleet from the active fleet. The congestion can be attributed to several factors rather than a single capacity constraint. Pilot shortages, prioritisation of higher-priority cargoes such as fuel, frequent air-raid alerts and weather-related interruptions have reduced the effective flow of vessels, leading to only three to four vessels transiting per day moving towards Ukraine, which could still take several weeks to clear. According to official data, Ukraine’s grain exports were down almost 70% YoY in August, illustrating the extent to which the disruption is affecting the country’s overall grain flows despite efforts to divert cargo to the Danube. However, it has handled much larger volumes in the past when Russia had blocked Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. Grain export capacity through the Danube reached about 2.5 million tonnes per month during 2022-23. However, current volumes remain well below those levels, highlighting congestion even before the route has returned to its previous peak throughput. Congestion supporting freight fundamentals The main impact has been a reduction in effective vessel supply. Extended waiting times have increased ballast and voyage inefficiencies, keeping vessels occupied without generating revenue. As congestion persists, owners are more likely to factor waiting-time risk into freight negotiations, while charterers face a shrinking pool of available fleet. Given the relatively concentrated deployment of sub-10,000 dwt vessels within the Black Sea, even modest increases in delays can have a massive impact on vessel availability, adding $7,000pd cost. This should continue to support regional voyage and time-charter rates in the small general cargo segment in this particular region. Grain export patterns favour smaller general cargo vessels The disruption is likely to hamper conventional dry-bulk demand, as a significant portion of cargo is being redirected via the Danube and carried by general cargo vessels. Draft restrictions and port infrastructure limitations mean cargoes previously moved on larger Handysize and Handymax bulkers are increasingly divided into smaller parcels. As a result, cargoes that would traditionally have been carried by dry-bulk vessels from deep-sea ports are increasingly being absorbed by smaller general-cargo vessels. This represents a degree of substitution away from conventional bulk tonnage, particularly for smaller parcel sizes. General cargo market outlook The implications are most pronounced for the general cargo fleet. Nearly one-quarter of the world’s sub-10,000 dwt fleet operates in the wider Black Sea market. Persistent congestion at Sulina is tightening vessel supply in a region that already plays a key role in grain and project cargo trades. If Ukrainian Danube export flows remain elevated, congestion is likely to sustain higher fleet utilisation and limit vessel availability throughout the grain export season; this points towards a positive outlook for regional general cargo earnings, with upside potential for both voyage and time-charter rates even without significant growth in overall cargo volumes. Photograph: Roses Nicolas/ABACA/Shutterstock France Letters France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb Amid widespread protests, Muriel E Cockcroft has sympathy for French youth but fears how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.39 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.41 EDT Share I’m writing in response to your editorial ( The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment, 19 October ). While the focus is on Emmanuel Macron, let us not forget the hierarchical structure of French administration, from mayors to MPs to senators to prefects and heads of region. All are part of the government, but few stood up to bring leaky school roofs and missing teachers to national consciousness. I deplore the senseless destruction of shops and state buildings. But I also deplore the fact that students had to protest to be heard. In the many administrative tiers of this highly hierarchical country, no one acted and inertia prevailed. Centrally, the government is financially challenged but refuses to acknowledge that having a huge deficit, an ageing population and a low retirement age are perhaps connected. Modest attempts to increase the retirement age also provoked violent protests. Financial tools for individual retirement remain complex and restricted. Thus, this sclerotic system presses on until the next crisis. Neither side of the populist fringe offers a viable path forward. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise actively avoid confronting the retirement timebomb, preferring politically expedient promises over fiscal reality. If a system treats retirement as a sacred cow even when the meaning of work is being redefined at lightning speed by AI, if it’s acceptable to have productivity grind to a halt in August because the wisdom of asking employees to all take four to five weeks off in the same month while we live in a 24/7 world is never questioned, and if that same system lets young people study by rote in leaky classrooms while offering its over-60s free social dinners, let us not be surprised if the pressure valve is showing signs of fatigue. My concern is how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: New Delhi: Union Minister Piyush Goyal on Tuesday held separate meetings with Czech Republic Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havliček and former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to discuss strengthening bilateral economic cooperation, trade, investment and technology partnerships.In a post on X, Goyal said he held a productive meeting with Havliček, during which both sides explored avenues to strengthen bilateral trade and investment, encourage joint manufacturing and industrial partnerships, and expand cooperation across key sectors. Explored avenues to strengthen bilateral trade & investment, encourage joint manufacturing & industrial partnerships, and expand cooperation in railways, mobility, defence & advanced technologies, Goyal said.He further emphasised the importance of closer industry-to-industry collaboration in strengthening the economic partnership and unlocking new opportunities through the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (India-EU FTA). We reaffirmed the role of closer industry-to-industry collaboration in strengthening our economic partnership and unlocking new opportunities through the India-EU FTA, Goyal added.In a separate post on X, Goyal expressed delight at meeting former UK Prime Minister Sunak, referring to him as his friend. Delighted to meet my friend and former UK Prime Minister, Goyal said.He added that the discussions focused on strengthening economic cooperation between India and the United Kingdom to drive growth, with trade, investment, innovation and technology partnerships featuring prominently in the exchange. It was a great exchange on strengthening India-UK economic cooperation to drive growth. Our discussions featured trade, investment, innovation, and technology partnerships between the two sides, Goyal said.The two meetings focused on expanding India's economic engagement with European partners, strengthening bilateral trade and investment, and creating opportunities for industrial collaboration, innovation and technological cooperation.Earlier on Tuesday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Karel Havliček reviewed the entire spectrum of defence industrial cooperation between the two countries and agreed to expand collaboration under the India-Czech Joint Defence Committee to promote 'Make in India' and 'Aatmanirbhar Bharat'.During their bilateral meeting in New Delhi, the two leaders welcomed the ongoing collaboration and the successful establishment of various joint ventures, while agreeing to further strengthen defence industrial ties, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Defence.Sharing details of the meeting on X, Rajnath Singh said, Had a wonderful meeting with the Vice Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade of the Czech Republic, Mr Karel Havlicek in New Delhi today. We reviewed the entire spectrum of Defence Industrial Cooperation, and we were pleased to note the progress and success of various Joint Ventures. We also agreed to further expand this collaboration under the aegis of the India-Czech Joint Defence Committee, to promote Atmanirbhar Bharat. Havliček is on a four-day visit to India and is holding interactions with various ministries, trade representatives and businesses. During his visit, he is also scheduled to travel to Bengaluru and Mumbai to visit industries.Meanwhile, Rishi Sunak also met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and congratulated the latter on completing 25 years in public service and hailed the UK-India partnership.In a post on X, Sunak recalled working with PM Modi during his tenure as UK PM and commended PM Modi's commitment and work ethic, calling it exemplary.Shedding light on the UK-India partnership, he said that the ties continue to strengthen under PM Modi's leadership, while expressing hopes for further bolstering of bilateral cooperation. Prime Minister @narendramodi great to see you in New Delhi today. Congratulations on 25 years in public service, a remarkable achievement.
